## Q1. Attrition rate for employees at BI:

```{r}
# attrition rate function
attrition_rate <- function(x) {
  mean(x == "Yes")
}
```

### Overall attrition rate

```{r}
# Overall attrition rate
attrition_rate(bioimplant$attrition)
```

### Summary Table

```{r}
# Conditional rates by department and job role
attrition_table <- bioimplant %>%
  group_by(department, job_role) %>%
  summarise(
    attrition_rate = attrition_rate(attrition),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(attrition_rate))

head(attrition_table)
```

## Q2. Logistic regression model of attrition using all predictors:

```{r}
# setting the binomial levels
bioimplant$attrition <- factor(bioimplant$attrition, levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# model using everything but employee_number
log_model <- glm(
  attrition ~ . - employee_number,
  data = bioimplant,
  family = binomial
)

# summary(log_model)

# Predict "Yes" when the predicted probability is at least 0.5
predicted_probability <- predict(log_model, type = "response")
predicted_class <- ifelse(predicted_probability >= 0.5, "Yes", "No")

# comparing predicted category with actual. Result is proportion of correctly classified
accuracy <- mean(predicted_class == as.character(bioimplant$attrition))
cat("Predicted accuracy:", round(accuracy, 4), "\n")


# Majority class accuracy: predict "No" for every employee
majority_accuracy <- mean(bioimplant$attrition == "No")
cat("Majority accuracy:", round(majority_accuracy, 4), "\n")
```

### Model vs predicted comparison:

The majority class accuracy os 0.8388 and the predicted accuracy of the model is 0.8925 improving the majority 0.0537 or 5.37 percentage points.

## Q3. Compare Attrition Predictors Using Standardized Logistic Regression Coefficients:

```{r}
# scaling the numeric data
bioimplant_scaled <- bioimplant %>%
  mutate(across(
    where(is.numeric),
    ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))
  ))

# another logistic regression using the scaled data removing employee_number and departmentı
scaled_log_model <- glm(
  attrition ~ . - employee_number,
  data = bioimplant_scaled,
  family = binomial
)

# summary(scaled_log_model)

# Find the largest coefficient by absolute value, excluding the intercept
# Extracting the coefficients
coefs <- coef(scaled_log_model)
# Removing the intercept
coefs <- coefs[names(coefs) != "(Intercept)"]
# Taking the absolute value, then finding the largest value, but preserves original value
coefs[which.max(abs(coefs))]
```

## Q4. The largest absolute coefficient was associated with the Human Resources job role. What change in predicted attrition does the model estimate if HR employees receive one additional training session per year, and why might training be a useful policy to examine?

```{r}
# Predict current attrition probabilities
p_current <- predict(scaled_log_model, type = "response")

# Scenario: HR employees receive one additional training session
training_policy <- bioimplant_scaled
hr_employees <- training_policy$job_role == "Human Resources"

training_sd <- sd(bioimplant$training_times_last_year, na.rm = TRUE)
training_max_scaled <- (max(bioimplant$training_times_last_year, na.rm = TRUE) -
  mean(bioimplant$training_times_last_year, na.rm = TRUE)) /
  training_sd

training_policy$training_times_last_year[hr_employees] <- pmin(
  training_policy$training_times_last_year[hr_employees] + 1 / training_sd,
  training_max_scaled
)

p_training_hr <- predict(
  scaled_log_model,
  newdata = training_policy,
  type = "response"
)

# Change in average predicted attrition probability for HR employees, in percentage points
100 * (mean(p_training_hr[hr_employees]) - mean(p_current[hr_employees]))

# Change in the company's average predicted attrition probability, in percentage points
100 * (mean(p_training_hr) - mean(p_current))
```

The model identifies the HR job role as the group to examine. I modeled a change where HR employees attended one additional training session. The model predicts a lower average attrition probability (-2.34 percentage points) under this scenario.

## Q5. What should Angelica say in her report? Please include quantitative details from your answers to the questions above.

BioImplants’ overall attrition rate is 16.1%. Attrition varies by job role: Sales Representatives had the highest observed rate at 39.8% (33 of 83 employees), while 23.1% of Human Resources employees left (12 of 52). These are observed rates and do not account for differences in other employee characteristics.

The logistic regression correctly classified 89.25% of employees, compared with 83.88% accuracy from predicting “No” for everyone—a 5.37 percentage-point difference. This is training accuracy because the model was evaluated on the same data used to fit it, so its performance on new employees may be lower.

The largest absolute coefficient was for the Human Resources job role, at +14.02 on the log-odds scale. This does not mean attrition increased by 14%. Because the estimate is unusually large, I would check the model diagnostics before treating it as a reliable measure. Sales Representatives had the highest observed attrition rate, so both groups may warrant further review.

In a model-based scenario, I increased training by one session for HR employees, up to the highest training value observed in the data. The model predicted a 2.34 percentage-point decrease in average attrition probability for HR employees and a 0.083 percentage-point decrease company-wide. These are estimates from the fitted model, not proof that training will cause attrition to fall. BioImplants could pilot the training policy for HR employees and compare actual results over time.
